name: Turquoise Green
lede: Turquoise green is a pale, cool mint green, and also the trade name of a chromium, aluminium and cobalt oxide pigment that is a good deal bluer than the swatch.

sections.title: The pigment
sections.body:
*Turquoise green* is a modern synthetic pigment, a chromium-aluminium-cobalt oxide [1][2]. The Colour Index (1971) lists it as CI 77343 and describes a recipe: a mixture of aluminium hydroxide, chromium oxide and cobalt carbonate, ignited at white heat [1].

The Pigment Compendium treats it as a synonym of Turkish green, because in German *türkis* and *türkisch* are the same word and English translators rendered it both ways [2][3]. German sources also call it *chromblaugrün*, chrome blue-green [2]. Its nearest relative in the paint box is [[cerulean-blue]], and a deeper blue-green neighbor is [[viridian]]. The Compendium notes that some modern acrylic paints labelled cerulean blue contain the same chromium-cobalt-aluminium oxide [1][2].

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.body: The pigment was in use by the mid nineteenth century. Recipes by Salvétat (1859) and Mierzinski (1881) are cited for it, and Zerr and Rübencamp's handbook of 1906 gave a mixture of 30 parts cobalt carbonate, 60 of aluminium hydrate and 30 of chromium oxide hydrate [2]. Schleich the Elder's Munich painting of 1862 is cited as a find of the same oxide mixture [2]. The oxide is otherwise rare, even in modern acrylics labelled cerulean blue [2].

sections.title: The swatch is not the pigment
sections.body: The color on this page is a pale mint, a name taken from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930, which dates a *turquoise green* to 1845, and from ISCC-NBS block 163 [4]. A pigment of this name is deeper and bluer, and RAL 6016 *Turquoise green*, a paint standard, is a dark teal that sits about as far from the swatch as a green can [4]. Treat the name as a family of blue-greens, not a single formula.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Within six units of CIEDE2000 and at least five per cent of the canvas, this mint green turns up in 12 of 23,781 museum paintings [5]. Three of the largest matches are by [[painter:vincent-van-gogh|Van Gogh]], including [[painting:nga-72328|Roses]], where it covers about 44 per cent of the picture [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test [5].

questions.q: Why do English books call the same pigment both Turkish green and turquoise green?
choices: German uses one word for both Turkish and turquoise
It was made in Turkey from turquoise stone
Two different pigments share the name
It was named after a Turkish painter
questions.answer: German uses one word for both Turkish and turquoise

questions.q: Which three oxides are fired together to make turquoise green pigment?

openers: Turquoise green the pigment is a chromium-cobalt-aluminium oxide fired at white heat; the mint swatch is only the name's pale cousin.
Look for the pale mint in Van Gogh's Roses, where it covers about 44 per cent of the canvas.
